summary: Defines an IPv4 option providing sender-directed multi-destination delivery, called Selective Directed Broadcast Mode (SDBM). It is historic and was replaced by RFC 6814.

plainLanguage.summary: The sender lists several receivers so one packet goes to just those.

how many addresses fit in the sdbm ip option
why does sdbm only work with udp
subtitle: An IPv4 option that lists up to nine destination addresses so one datagram can reach just those hosts.

tldr.problem: A sender sometimes needs to deliver one message to a small, specific set of hosts without any group-membership control traffic, which matters on bandwidth-constrained tactical military networks.
tldr.mechanism: The sender puts the addresses of the wanted hosts in an IPv4 option, sends the datagram to the network's directed broadcast address, and each host processes it only if its own address is in the list.
tldr.outcome: SDBM provides unreliable UDP delivery only, with reliability left to the application. The RFC is Historic and was replaced by RFC 6814.

today: RFC 1770 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 6814. It was published as an Informational memo and never specified an Internet standard.

sections.title: Purpose and Background
sections.content:
This Informational memo defines an IPv4 option for Selective Directed Broadcast Mode (SDBM). It gives unreliable UDP delivery to a set of IP addresses carried in the option field of an IPv4 datagram. If data reliability is required, the application layer provides it, for example with acknowledgements.

The design was developed for sender-directed delivery to sparsely populated groups with no additional control traffic. SDBM is part of the U.S. Army standard for tactical data communication networks, MIL-STD-188-220, and the author expects it to suit the extremely bandwidth-constrained tactical military environment as well as some commercial uses.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a sender wants to tell only a few friends something. Instead of shouting to everybody, it writes the friends' names on the message.

sections.title: The SDBM Option Format
sections.content:
The option has a TYPE octet, a LENGTH octet, and then the destination IP addresses, 4 octets each. IP options are limited to 40 octets by the header length field, so the option can use 38 octets: 2 for the control fields and room for at most 9 addresses.

The TYPE field holds the copy flag, the class and the option number. The class is 0 and the option number is 21. The copy bit should be set to 1 so that the address list is copied into every fragment, which gives a TYPE value of 149. The length is calculated as 2 + 4*(number of IP addresses).
sections.plainLanguage: The note on the packet says how long the list is and then lists each friend's address, up to nine of them.

sections.title: Sending and Routing SDBM Datagrams
sections.content:
A source host groups the destination hosts by network ID. Each network gets at least one directed broadcast datagram, and a network with more than 9 destinations needs several. The destination address of each datagram is the directed broadcast address of that network, and the source address is the sender's own. Up to 9 full destination addresses go in the option. If other IP options are present, the number of addresses must shrink to fit within the 40 octets.

Transit routers handle the datagram as any ordinary IP datagram. The router attached to the destination network chooses one of three ways to deliver it. If the subnet can broadcast, it broadcasts and lets hosts filter by address. If it cannot broadcast, it sends a separate local packet to each listed host. If the subnet has reliable layer 2 multi-address capability, as MIL-STD-188-220 networks do, it uses one layer 2 multi-address frame.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender sorts friends by neighborhood and sends one note per neighborhood. The last post office either shouts it out, delivers it to each house, or uses a special group delivery if it has one.

sections.title: Receiving and Limits
sections.content:
A receiving host looks inside the option for its own address and keeps processing the datagram only if it finds it. This gives the source explicit control over which hosts process the datagram.

Because the destination address is a broadcast address, SDBM can be used only with UDP and not with TCP, which supports only point-to-point connections. The memo says nothing about security: its Security Considerations section states that security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: Everybody on the street hears the message, but only the people named on it act on it. It works for quick notes, not for long phone calls.
